title: Decidability of freeness in automaton groups
formal: Is abstract freeness of an automaton group decidable? Does one deterministic Turing machine, given any finite complete deterministic invertible Mealy automaton \(\mathcal A\), always halt and return YES exactly when \[\exists r\in\mathbb N\quad G(\mathcal A)\cong F_r,\] where \(G(\mathcal A)\) is generated by all state transformations and their inverses and \(F_r\) is the free group of rank \(r\)? Rank zero, the trivial group, is included. The question does not require the supplied state transformations themselves to be a free basis.
why: Automata give finite descriptions of groups that can have complex infinite structure and need not have finite presentations by relations. Recognizing a free group tests a fundamental structural property in this representation. The problem isolates the effect of invertibility on decidability and distinguishes structural recognition from equality of individual represented elements.
status_note: The MFCS 2024 final section and the 12 March 2026 St Andrews handout explicitly retain abstract automaton group freeness as open. The original §7.2.1(b) and current definition quantify over some free basis, not necessarily the input states. Positive-relations undecidability and general semigroup/monoid freeness do not resolve this predicate. The search through 16 September 2026 found no matching later resolution and is not exhaustive.

category_assignment.reason: The main property is freeness of a group given by an automaton presentation.

importance.reason: A longstanding structural decision problem for automaton groups, explicitly retained after the 2024 semigroup/monoid breakthrough and in a specialist March 2026 presentation.

sentences: A finite invertible Mealy machine describes bijections of all finite words, whose compositions and inverses form an automaton group.
The question asks for an always-terminating algorithm deciding whether that whole group is isomorphic to a free group of some finite rank.
The supplied states may be redundant or act trivially, so they are not required to form the free basis.
Known undecidability of positive relations and of general automaton semigroup freeness does not settle this group property, which a March 2026 specialist presentation still lists as open.
A resolution would locate a basic limit of structural recognition from finite automaton descriptions.

definitions:
A finite complete deterministic Mealy automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,\lambda)\), with finite nonempty state set \(Q\), finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and total tables \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\), \(\lambda:Q\times\Sigma\to\Sigma\). Invertibility means that for each state \(q\), the map \(a\mapsto\lambda(q,a)\) is a permutation of \(\Sigma\). No reversibility assumption is made on the maps \(q\mapsto\delta(q,a)\), and the numbers of states and letters are unbounded parts of the input. There are no designated initial or accepting states: all states are generators. The input is the full finite table, with binary state/letter indices and cardinalities. Invalid or noninvertible tables may be rejected.

The set \(\Sigma^*\) contains all finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Each state defines a transformation recursively by \(T_q(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\) and \(T_q(aw)=\lambda(q,a)T_{\delta(q,a)}(w)\). Invertibility makes each \(T_q\) a bijection of \(\Sigma^*\), preserving lengths and prefixes. The group \(G(\mathcal A)\) consists of all finite compositions of these functions and their inverses, including the empty composition, with function composition as multiplication. Equality means agreement on every finite input word of every length. This uses synchronous, total, one-letter-in/one-letter-out machines, rather than partial or asynchronous transducers.

The free group \(F_r\) has generators \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) and their formal inverses. Its elements are finite reduced words, meaning adjacent inverse pairs have been cancelled; multiplication concatenates words and cancels such pairs, the empty word is the identity, and inversion reverses the word and flips each sign. Freeness of \(G(\mathcal A)\) means existence of a bijection to this group preserving multiplication and identity. A possible free basis may consist of arbitrary group elements rather than the given state list, which can contain identities, duplicates or dependent generators. Since the group is finitely generated, allowing all finite ranks is sufficient; no basis, rank, isomorphism or bound on relation length is supplied as an input promise or required as output.

The target is exact uniform decidability on every valid automaton table, with termination on both free and nonfree cases and no resource bound. One ordinary algorithm must work for all input sizes. No oracle, nonuniform advice, randomness, numerical tolerance or restriction to bounded input-word lengths is allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that this predicate admits a total computable decider on the encoded complete invertible Mealy tables, or prove that it does not. The formalization must connect the state recursion, generated group of all-word transformations and existence of an abstract free-group isomorphism, including rank zero, to the algorithm's correctness and termination. A negative reduction must preserve complete deterministic invertibility. Deciding whether the named states freely generate, checking absence of a positive relation, or proving semigroup freeness undecidable does not by itself meet the abstract group target. Failure of one bounded relation search is not a proof that every total algorithm is impossible. The card review does not claim a verified Lean resolution.

source_formulation.text: Is there an algorithm deciding whether the group generated by a given complete invertible finite automaton is a free group?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the abstract group-freeness question

context_blocks.text: A state table supplies a compact recursive description of transformations on a rooted tree of all finite words. Deciding equality of two specified products is possible in this representation, but recognizing the abstract structure of the entire infinite group is a separate problem.

The original 2000 list asks about the group’s structural properties, and the March 2026 handout defines freeness as isomorphism to a free group over some basis. This confirms that the target is not an injectivity test for the map from the free group on the names of all states.

For example, the usual adding machine generates an infinite cyclic group together with an identity state. The group is free of rank one, while the given state list is not a free basis and already contains a positive relation because the identity state acts trivially. Redundant state generators must therefore not force a NO answer.

Theorem 3.7 of the 2020 paper proves undecidability of checking absence of positive relations, which are nonempty products of state generators acting as the identity without using inverses. The same paper explicitly distinguishes this presentation-dependent property from abstract group freeness. Its appended erratum retracts other freeness claims, and was checked with the theorem.

The MFCS 2024 result proves undecidability of freeness for general complete automaton semigroups and monoids. Its final section still lists automaton group freeness as open. Allowing noninvertible state actions in the negative construction is not the promised group input class.

The 12 March 2026 specialist handout again records group freeness as open while listing semigroup/monoid freeness as undecidable. A bounded search through September found no checked later resolution; the card reports this dated evidence rather than claiming an exhaustive status proof.
